title: What sparse autoencoders don’t tell you about a circuit
text: A sparse autoencoder gives you a dictionary of directions in activation space and a claim that those directions are more interpretable than neurons. That claim is doing a lot of work, and this note is about where it stops holding.

title: What sparse autoencoders don’t tell you about a circuit
text:
The setup
Given activations \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), an SAE learns an encoder and decoder such that
\[
\hat{x} = W_{\text{dec}} f(x) + b, \qquad f(x) = \text{ReLU}(W_{\text{enc}}(x - b)),
\]
trained to minimise reconstruction error under an \(\ell_1\) penalty on \(f(x)\):
\[
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\lVert x - \hat{x} \rVert_2^2}_{\text{reconstruction}} + \lambda \underbrace{\lVert f(x) \rVert_1}_{\text{sparsity}}.
\]
The interpretability claim is that the columns of \(W_{\text{dec}}\) correspond to human-legible features (Cunningham et al., 2023). The mechanistic claim — which is different, and stronger — is that those features are the units the model itself computes over (Olah et al., 2020).

title: What sparse autoencoders don’t tell you about a circuit
section: Where the two claims come apart
text:
Where the two claims come apart






NoteThe short version



A dictionary element can be legible to you and still not be a variable the model uses. Legibility is a property of the projection; causal relevance has to be tested separately.


Three things to check before treating a feature as mechanistic:

Ablation actually changes behaviour. If zeroing the feature leaves the downstream logits untouched, you have found a correlate, not a cause.
The effect survives a better baseline. Mean ablation and zero ablation disagree, sometimes badly — I wrote about this separately.
The feature is stable across seeds. Dictionaries trained on the same activations with different seeds should recover overlapping features. Often they don’t.

title: What sparse autoencoders don’t tell you about a circuit
text:
A quick illustration



import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

l0 = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128])
mse = np.array([0.42, 0.27, 0.16, 0.11, 0.09, 0.085])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.2))
ax.plot(l0, mse, marker="o", color="#11707E")
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
ax.set_xlabel("mean $L_0$ (active features per token)")
ax.set_ylabel("reconstruction MSE")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()

title: What sparse autoencoders don’t tell you about a circuit
section: What I’d want to see next
text:
What I’d want to see next
An SAE paper that reports, for its headline features, the ablation effect size alongside the interpretability score. Right now those two numbers rarely appear in the same table.

title: A one-GPU setup for interpretability experiments
text: Most of what I run fits on a single GPU if the activations never all exist at once. The pattern below is what I keep coming back to.

title: A one-GPU setup for interpretability experiments
section: Hook once, write straight to disk
text:
Hook once, write straight to disk

from contextlib import contextmanager
import torch

@contextmanager
def capture(module, store, key):
    """Append this module's output to `store[key]`, on CPU, then detach."""
    def hook(_m, _inp, out):
        store.setdefault(key, []).append(out.detach().to("cpu", torch.float16))
    handle = module.register_forward_hook(hook)
    try:
        yield store
    finally:
        handle.remove()

Two details do most of the work: float16 on the way out halves the disk cost with no visible effect on anything I’ve measured, and .to("cpu") inside the hook keeps the GPU from accumulating a batch’s worth of residual stream.

title: A one-GPU setup for interpretability experiments
text:
Three habits worth the friction

One run, one directory, one config file. If you can’t reconstruct which checkpoint produced a figure, the figure isn’t evidence.
Save the tokenizer output, not just the text. Re-tokenizing later with a slightly different version is a silent source of mismatch.
Write the negative results down the same day. They are the ones you will otherwise re-run in four months.

title: About
text:
Who I am · What I work on

I’m a computer science PhD student at UC Santa Barbara. My research interests sit at the intersection of AI safety and reasoning: interpretability methods that scale, alignment techniques that survive contact with capable models, and the question of whether a model’s stated reasoning has anything to do with its real computation.
Before this I worked on generative models, machine unlearning for LLMs, physics-informed neural networks and reinforcement learning. Those threads still show up here — unlearning in particular turns out to be an interpretability problem wearing a different hat.
I’m currently looking for research internships and preparing PhD applications in AI safety. If you’re working on something adjacent, I’d like to hear about it.
